Displaced Palestinians react at a partially flooded tent camp during a rainy day in Gaza City. [Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 25 Nov 202625 Nov 2026
Gaza’s municipalities have warned that winter rains could flood about 1,000 camps and other sites hosting displaced Palestinians in the war-torn enclave, adding that damage to drains and sewers, and a shortage of pumps, have left their crews with little means to clear the water.
After a meeting in Gaza City on Wednesday, the Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities singled out al-Mughraqa and al-Zahra in central Gaza, where water levels in Wadi Gaza could rise suddenly. Across the territory, about 200,000 tents need replacing, and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse, the union said. Gaza’s Government Media Office had warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days.

This is Gaza’s fourth winter since Israel launched its war in October 2023. The union said storms in early November flooded about 70,000 tents and affected more than 350,000 displaced people. During a winter storm this November, families piled sand at tent entrances to keep out the rain. Others carried their children out and salvaged what belongings they could.
One displaced mother said she had cut up the burial shroud she had bought for her son and used it to patch her tent. She wanted to keep the family’s bedding and clothes dry. “I couldn’t get a tarpaulin,” she said.

The US Department of Education building is seen in Washington, DC on November 18, 2024 [Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo]By Umar FarooqPublished On 25 Nov 202625 Nov 2026
The United States Department of Education says it is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a district in the state of Virginia after local officials shut down all of its schools in the wake of a child sexual abuse scandal involving its employees.
“Parents should never have to question whether their child’s school is aiding and abetting child predators,” US Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said in a statement on Tuesday. “The Trump Administration is taking decisive enforcement action to hold those responsible accountable and ensure Virginia schools are safe places for children to learn.”
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3US universities brace for education policies overhaul under Trumplist 2 of 3Donald Trump signs executive order to ‘eliminate’ Department of Educationlist 3 of 3University of Virginia president resigns under US government pressureend of list
Officials in Albemarle County, Virginia, announced they were closing all 29 schools in the district last week, after learning that more than 500 staff had not been subjected to a routine background screening for a history of child sexual abuse. The school system has about 2,800 employees, and only a fraction of its $284m budget comes from the federal government.
Local officials emphasised that none of the 524 employees is suspected of abuse.
Approximately 14,000 students attend the schools, and parents have scrambled to find childcare, while many who depend on free school meals for their children have had to look for other sources of food.

Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during the parliamentary meeting of the Israeli parliament (Knesset) in Jerusalem [AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 25 Nov 202625 Nov 2026
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for an immediate end to his long-running corruption trial after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping a case in which he is accused of bribery.
Netanyahu on Wednesday said the “fabricated cases” against him were falling apart, in a televised statement at the Israeli parliament.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form governmentlist 2 of 4Could Netanyahu take Israel into another war with Iran to cling to power?list 3 of 4Knesset advances October 7 probe despite Netanyahu’s objectionslist 4 of 4The ‘eighth front’: Why Israel’s influence war in the US is failingend of list
The judges’ recommendations came as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival after inconclusive October 27 elections.
Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, has been tasked with forming a government, and if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence.
“Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family,” Netanyahu said in his speech.
“Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul. Who will give those years back to us?”
“The trial must end immediately,” he added.
During a hearing in Jerusalem on Wednesday regarding three corruption cases against Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported.

Smoke and debris is sent into the air after the US Army detonated lead azide in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, USA, 25 November 2026 [Matthew Putney/EPA]By Hoda SherifPublished On 25 Nov 202625 Nov 2026
United States Army officials have hailed Wednesday’s mission to destroy 68 drums of volatile lead azide — a sensitive munitions explosive — at a military base in Iowa as a success, saying it had “wildly exceeded their expectations”.
Speaking at a news conference in Middletown, a southeastern rural city adjacent to the ammunition plant where the operation was carried out, Major General Eric Shirley, the Army official in charge of the disposal effort, said overhead footage showed that “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed”.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Trump delays explosive detonation in US state of Iowa amid legal battleslist 2 of 4US army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed Wednesdaylist 3 of 4US Army to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesdaylist 4 of 4US Army detonates toxic lead explosives in Iowa amid health concernsend of list
The controlled detonation at 10:15am (16:15 GMT) destroyed approximately 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I.
“There was no secondary explosions. There was no kick-out. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley said, adding that the operation was “tremendously successful”.
Officials also said that extensive mitigation measures, including earthworks, foam barriers and gel blocks, had helped to absorb the shockwaves and toxic fallout.
